title: Drive your own nail with a hammer another robot arm also needs
instruction: Use the hammer to drive the nail in front of you into its block, leave the other nail alone, and put the hammer back down for the other arm.
context: Workers who share one tool have to wait for it, use it on their own job only and hand it back. This checks that a policy can do that beside a second arm that wants the same hammer and cannot be talked to.
setup: A 90 x 90 cm wooden table top, 75 cm high. Two YAM arms stand side by side at the back edge, 50 cm apart; the controlled arm is the right one in the screenshot. Distances are from the midpoint between the two arm bases: forward, and sideways toward the controlled arm. A small hammer, 130 g in all: a 26 cm wooden handle with a flat-sided rubber grip, 20 x 24 mm, and a 3 x 3 x 7 cm steel head. It stands on its face on the centre line with the middle of its handle 20 cm forward, the head away from the arms and the handle level, its near end on a wooden rest block 10 cm forward. Two wooden blocks, 8 x 8 x 3 cm, each with a steel nail standing 2.5 cm out of its middle (20 mm head): one 30 cm forward and 25 cm toward the controlled arm, the other 30 cm forward and 25 cm toward the other arm. The other arm waits a set time, takes the hammer when it lies free and the controlled arm is not reaching for it, drives the other nail, and puts the hammer back where it started. It does the same in every trial.
scoring: The depth the nail in front of the controlled arm goes in while that arm holds the hammer, over 17 mm (the head within 8 mm of the wood), up to 1; halved if the controlled arm still holds the hammer at the end. 0 if the two arms ever touch, or if the controlled arm drives the other nail; the run stops at the first touch or wrong blow.
reset_notes: Put the hammer back on its face and rest, and pull both nails back up to stand 2.5 cm out of their blocks.
fidelity: Approximate. Each nail rides a slide held by 50 N of friction and only the hammer can push it; a resting hammer does not move it. Arm links collide as fitted capsules slightly larger than the real ones, so a near miss under about 1 cm can count as a touch. The gripper pinches with up to 50 N through flat pads. The controller uses the manufacturer's joint gains, gravity compensation and motor torque-speed limits. The other arm is scripted on the true scene state.
